generatedProse.concept-context: Many subjects in the School of Sport use APA style, set by the American Psychological Association, while coaching, management and some applied modules may use Harvard; your department will tell you which. Whatever the style, a reference is built from the same parts: the author's surname and initial, the year, the title, and where the work was published. Each style sets its own rules for how these parts are punctuated and arranged. Once you can see the parts, a reference stops looking like a jumble and you can both read it and build your own.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students need to reference the same coaching journal article.

Tom copies a ready-made reference from the library's discovery service and pastes it in, then copies another from a PDF for the next source. One gives the year in brackets, the other does not, and the author initials are formatted differently; Tom does not notice. The parts are all there somewhere, but the list mixes layouts and no single pattern holds.

Amara builds each reference from its parts: the author's surname and initial, then the year in brackets, the article title, the journal in italics, and the volume and pages, all in the style her department asks for. Because she can see the parts, every reference follows the same pattern and a reader can scan the list with confidence.

Both students had the same sources. Only Amara recognised the parts and the style, and produced a reference list that holds together.
generatedProse.summary: The School of Sport leans on APA in many of its subjects, but the point holds for any style; every reference is built from the same parts, the author, date, title and publication details, arranged by the conventions of the style. You can now recognise that subjects use different styles, identify the parts of a reference, and say that much of the school uses APA. The next lesson is about using a style accurately when you quote and paraphrase.

check.body: In the worked example, what let Amara produce a reference list that held together?

items.text: She built each reference from its parts and kept to one style throughout.
She pasted ready-made references from the discovery service.
She used more studies than Tom did.
She chose a different layout for each reference.

feedback.correct: That's right. Building each reference from its parts and keeping to one style made the list consistent.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did that Tom did not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara built each reference from its parts and kept to one style. Pasting ready-made references, piling up studies or mixing layouts all work against a consistent list.
